newsitem.title: USA: FBI tapes record Florida bond bribery talk.
newsitem.headline: FBI tapes record Florida bond bribery talk.

text.p: FBI videotapes show the former president of a California municipal bond firm offering a Dade County, Fla., official a $300,000 kickback in exchange for steering bond business to the firm, The Miami Herald reported Thursday.

The tape recorded a meeting between Calvin Grigsby, who resigned from the San Francisco firm Grigsby Brandford & Co on Sept 17, in a hotel room with Dade County Commissioner James Burke, who previously chaired the county's finance committee.
The conversation took place last month in a San Francisco hotel, the Mark Hopkins, where Burke, Grigsby and Miami bond firm owner Howard Gary discussed the kickbacks, the newspaper said.

Grigsby offered to pay Burke when the $183 million revenue bond refunding issue closed on Sept 10, the newspaper said. The Herald said the money was to come from the fees earned by Grigsby Brandford & Co, which was the senior managing underwriter for the bond issue.
Gary's firm, Howard Gary & Co, was also part of the underwriting syndicate for the bond deal.
A spokesman at Howard Gary & Co, citing company policy, declined to comment.
Grigsby Brandford & Co said it would have no comment on Grigsby or his resignation "except to say that we have both chosen paths of separate and challenging responsibilities."
Burke and the FBI did not return Reuter calls.
However, Burke told The Herald that he was aware of the videotape's existence and that "You should ask who's doing the talking. Mostly it's Gary who is doing the orchestrating."
The newspaper reported previously that Gary was cooperating with federal investigators and had worn a hidden wire to record conversations implicating Burke in corruption related to Dade bond deals.
Because of the allegations, Howard Gary & Co, was pulled from an upcoming Dade County seaport deal on Wednesday.
No charges have been filed against Burke, Grigsby or Gary. Burke has denied wrongdoing and remains a county commissioner. Gary and Grigsby have declined comment, as did federal officials.

Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc, which is one of the nation's largest minority-owned investment banking firms, said on Thursday the firm maintains a solid financial condition and is moving forward with new business following Grigsby's resignation.
The firm said in a statement that it was in the process of restructuring its partnership interest.
"We are confident that over the next weeks and months Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc will continue to demonstrate its solid position and contribution to the municipal marketplace," the firm said.

California elections regulators revealed Wednesday that a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission official in Miami had asked them for information about campaign contrigutions by Grigsby to Florida public officials.
The move suggests that SEC staff in Miami has launched a probe of Dade County, Fla., bond deals involving Grigsby.
Charles Senatore, the SEC's regional director in Miami, declined to comment.
